# SK1040 — Use `T?` instead of `Nullable<T>`

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A bound `System.Nullable<T>` is written in long form where `T?` names exactly the same type.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

`T?` is the spelling every other nullable in the file already uses, so the long form reads as though it meant something different. It is also the form older samples and generated code produce, which is why an assistant writes it: the training data is full of `Nullable<int>` and the language stopped needing it in C# 2.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
Nullable<int> total = null;
```

Write:

```csharp
int? total = null;
```

## When it does not fire

The name is bound before anything is reported, so a user-defined `Nullable<T>` is never touched. Positions where the short form is not legal syntax are excluded rather than rewritten: the unbound `typeof(Nullable<>)`, a `cref` or `nameof` argument, a `using` alias, a member-access receiver, a pointer element type, and any pattern or `is` type test, because C# rejects a nullable value type in a pattern. Comments and preprocessor directives inside the type name are excluded because the rewrite deletes the text they live in. ⚠ **The fix is not safe (#412's audit, measured by running both versions):** An argument bound to a `[CallerArgumentExpression]` parameter (`Debug.Assert` on .NET 9+, `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull`, test asserts) captures its source text, and the rewrite changes the captured string. Only SK1025 consults `CallerArgumentSafety.CapturesText`.
